blocks.text: In the Aruch, Rabbi Judah explains ברבורים barburim as מיני ביברים, kinds of those animals that are kept in vivaria. This is very ambiguous. It is uncertain whether he means fish, birds or wild beasts. For although the Hebrew ביבר bibar, Greek βιβάριον [bibarion] (French vivier), is taken by the Hebrews ^{c)} and Greeks ^{d)} of a later age for a fishpond, the word vivarium once extended much more widely. Its scope, namely, embraced any enclosures in which living animals were fed. Thus Gellius, book 2, chapter 20, distinguishes three kinds of vivaria: aviaries (les volieres), hare-warrens (les garennes) and fishponds (les estangs). From the same author, however, it may be gathered that vivaria rather concerned wild beasts, like the παράδεισοι [paradeisoi] of the Greeks. “Vivaria,” he says, “as they are now called, are certain enclosed places in which wild beasts are fed alive.” Likewise: “The vivaria, as the common people now say, are what the Greeks call παραδείσους [paradeisous].” The Hebrews define exactly so what a ביבר bibar is. Aruch: ביבר הוא פרדס שמאספין שם חיות וחפירה שמאספין שם דגין ומקום מקורה ששם עופות, “A bibar is a park in which wild beasts are gathered; also a pit in which fish are collected; and finally a roofed place in which there are birds.” This is taken from the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, chapter 13, folio 106b, where the Gemara says: ביברין של חיות ושל עופות ושל דגין אין צדין מהם ביום טוב, “From bibarin (or vivaria) of wild beasts, birds and fish one may not hunt on a festival day.” Therefore the explanation of R. Judah, by which he defines ברבורים barburim as kinds of animals that are kept in vivaria, is far too broad. I add that it is hardly safe, because it rests entirely on a most empty play on the name. For R. Judah thought that ביבר bibar and ברבור barbur were words of the same origin, and hence that ביבר bibar was said for ברבר birbar, the letter Resh after the first being dropped, in the way Lamed has disappeared in the Chaldee or Syriac words ܓܓܘܠܬܐ, and ܩܝܩܘܠܬܐ, and ܨܘܨܠܬܐ, and ܫܘܫܠܬܐ. Yet it is perfectly plain that the Hebrew ביבר bibar, the Greek βιβάριον [bibarion], the Spanish bivar and the French vivier derive from the Roman word vivarium. Nevertheless, following this view, Castalio rendered the passage we are dealing with thus: “His provision for each day was thirty cors of fine flour,” etc., “besides harts, roes, wild oxen and vivaria.” In this respect, however, he is more inept than the Hebrews, since he put vivaria for the animals that are kept in vivaria. That is utterly absurd. For vivaria themselves are not [col. 129] among foods; nor would they be called אבוסים, fattened. And so Castalio passed over this word entirely untouched. Note in passing that in the Aruch the passage of R. Judah in which he explains the Hebrew ברברים as מיני ביברים is cited from Vayikra Rabbah, the chapter וכי ימוך אחיך, [II, 700] which is the thirty-fourth. Yet it appears nowhere there in the Venice edition of 1545, the only one I have been able to see. So either the Aruch is mistaken, or this edition is defective.

The third interpretation is that of those for whom ברברים barburim are birds in general, as if אברברים abarburim, from אבר eber, that is, from wing. This seems to be followed by Josephus, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Vulgate, R. Levi and Mordecai. So in their opinion ברבור barbur would stand for אברבר abarbur, of the pattern of אספסף asapsuph. But it is almost without precedent for the first radical to drop out of nouns formed from quiescent Pe Aleph verbs.
